title: Everything anyone asked for, between 1961 and now
material: About 2.1 million completed reader request slips in forty-two steel drawers: a shelfmark, a seat number, a date, and the reader's own handwriting on each. Sixty-five years of them, filed in the order they came back to the desk. The drawers are on a floor being given over to plant. Also: the empty forms, which are not confidential and of which there are boxes; the drawer labels; and the pulping contract, signed, for 14 January.
occasion: The board voted four to two to destroy them and will not revisit it. The contract is signed. Every particular that makes the slips worth anything — the hand, the date, the shelfmark — belongs to a reader and cannot be used, so the material is simultaneously entirely present and entirely unavailable, for five more weeks.
when: The drawers are emptied on 14 January. The vote was in June. There are five weeks left after installation.
where: The entrance hall of the library, which is a thoroughfare rather than a destination, and where nobody has ever stopped for anything.
means: The library's own workshop, which has one process it is confident in and two weeks in December between other jobs. Their stock and their machine. Nothing bought in: there is no cash, only materials already on the shelf.
atStake: Nothing made here changes the date. The slips go on 14 January regardless. What is unsettled is whether sixty-five years of a building's actual use is registered by anyone at all before the record of it stops existing, or whether it goes quietly because the only people who knew were the ones who filed them.
fear: That it turns into a campaign, that the campaign fails because the contract is signed, and that the last honest thing anyone could have said about the slips gets spent on a fight that was already lost in June.
pressures: 2.1 million wants to be shown as a quantity, and quantity is the one thing about this that is easy to make impressive, which is why it will read as a boast about the institution rather than as a loss.

The handwriting is the whole of it and none of it can be used. Everything pulls towards a substitute hand, an invented slip, a plausible shelfmark, and every one of those is a forgery of the exact thing that was worth keeping.
The endowment that paid for the floor conversion wants naming, at a specified size, because the same endowment is being asked for the next thing.
Nobody stops in this hall. That pulls hard towards whatever stops people, and whatever stops people in a thoroughfare is a device that would work equally well for anything.
refusals: No shelfmark, no seat number, no date belonging to an identifiable request, and nothing traceable to a reader. Reader confidentiality removes the only specific material there is and it is not negotiable for a good cause.

Not a reproduction of the handwriting, and not an imitation of it. A convincing forgery of a reader's hand is worse than saying nothing, because it is the loss being staged by the people responsible for it.
Not the word destroyed: legal permit only deaccessioned, which nobody outside the building understands. Both words are unavailable, one by rule and one by uselessness.
Nothing that asks anyone to do something about it. The contract is signed and an appeal that cannot be answered is a way of feeling active while the drawers empty on schedule.
notes: The workshop foreman has offered to keep one drawer at his own house. Nobody has said yes and nobody has said no.
